course_title: Advanced Writing: Grammar, Syntax and Style
course_description:
This course presents contemporary grammatical and stylistic concepts and strategies that will enhance students' ability to revise and edit their writing.

Welcome to Advanced Writing: Grammar, Syntax and Style , which will introduce you to contemporary models of English grammar and help you apply this explicit knowledge to both writing and editing tasks.

Throughout the semester, we will build on your intuitive understanding of how sentences work by discovering the form and function of the 9 English word classes and the ways we can combine structural elements to achieve improved clarity – and a variety of stylistic effects.

The lecture materials, tutorial activities, assessment items, and other course resources incorporate a variety of text types and writing styles so you can develop the vocabulary, tools, and confidence to use what you have learnt in a range of writing and editing contexts. We operate according to a #toolsnotrules ethos in which we understand sentence-level grammar as a series of patterns and relationships – rather than a value judgement – that can enhance the ways we think and talk about writing techniques and editorial decisions.

By participating actively in this course, you will have the opportunity to engage deeply and thoughtfully with the raw materials of written English and sharpen your approaches to writing and editing.

We look forward to learning with you this semester!

CLASS DELIVERY

This course is delivered in face-to-face mode, but it includes some online activities, alongside an abundance of extension material available to you in the Learning Resources folders on Blackboard.

You will get the most out of WRIT7260 if you commit to weekly attendance and participation. Students who come to class week by week typically approach their assessment with greater clarity and confidence – and they develop lasting friendships and professional connections with their classmates.

Please email Amber at a.gwynne@uq.edu.au if you would like to discuss any aspect of this course, including whatever access requirements and adjustments we can make to help ensure you get the most out of your study.

assessment_details.task_description: The discussion component of this course evaluates how well you have understood the concepts covered in readings, lectures, and classes throughout the semester and how well you can recognise particular structures, written conventions, and potential errors. The task has been designed to encourage deep weekly engagement with course content and meaningful discussion among your peers. You will participate in 10 online discussions across the semester. In each discussion thread, you will respond to a prompt and/or a classmate's contribution, receiving a mark between 1 and 3 depending on the accuracy and quality of your contribution. (Students who provide a substantial response – that is, demonstrate care and effort – should receive 3/3.) Each discussion will open the same day as your lecture and remain open for 7 days, closing at 4.00 pm before the following week's lecture. Read full task description Hide full task description

assessment_details.task_description: This in-class assessment gives you an opportunity to apply your developing knowledge of English structure and style to a sample of published text. On Monday morning ahead of the test date, you will gain access to a short passage of text, giving you an opportunity to annotate it and reflect on some of the ways the author has used words, phrases, and clauses (forms and structures) to achieve a particular style or effect. You may bring your annotated passage to the tutorial problem set, as well as one A4 page of notes and a print dictionary. The tutorial problem set lasts for 90 minutes: The first 10 minutes gives you perusal time, in which you can make initial notes about the three questions. You will then have 20 minutes to discuss your observations and impressions with classmates. The written component of this task then involves answering 3 questions about the text in paragraph form. You will have one hour (60 minutes) to write up your answers using the Inspera platform on your laptop. Read full task description Hide full task description

assessment_details.title: Editing task
assessment_details.task_description: The final editing task gives you an opportunity to apply what you have learnt throughout the semester to an activity you might encounter in the workplace (or as a professional editor): marking up a passage of text with corrections and advice to the author. This task is based loosely on the IPEd test for editors seeking accreditation in Australia. It's an excellent opportunity to gauge your current skill and accuracy as a writing and editing professional. The task comprises 10 sequential blocks of text that contain a total of 30 errors or obvious weaknesses. Your answer sheet will provide space for you to identify and describe each error or problem (for example, ‘spelling error—spell as X instead’ or ‘run-on sentence—insert semicolon’). Each note is worth one mark for a total of 30/40 marks. Your answer sheet will also provide space for you to re-write the entire passage to eliminate errors and improve clarity, tone, and structure, for a total of 10/40 marks. To submit your assignment, you should upload your completed answer sheet and submit it via Turnitin. Please make sure your answers are as specific and coherent as possible. (Remember: imagine you are describing the problem to a client.) Read full task description Hide full task description

learning_activities.topic: Week 1: Welcome to WRIT7260 Read the Course Profile and check out the Blackboard site. Watch the YouTube video about the history of English in only 10 minutes. AHEAD OF CLASS, WATCH THIS PRIMER VIDEO Why sentences? FACE-TO-FACE LECTURE Course overview, objectives, and assessment structure A brief history of English grammar education and its evolution Why does sentence-level grammar matter for professional writers and editors? Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04
Week 1: NO TUTORIAL

Week 2: More than words – voice, diction, style To prepare for classes this week, read the resources published in the Week 2 folder. Download a copy of the WRIT7260 glossary to add to throughout semester. BEFORE CLASS, WATCH THESE PRIMER VIDEOS Why and how are words the building blocks of English sentences, and why does word order matter so much? How do we put words into categories or classes? FACE-TO-FACE LECTURE This lecture introduces you to the principles of audience awareness, genre sensitivity, and individual voice. It addresses the importance of word choice not only to convey meanings but also to craft a particular voice, persona, tone, style, and effect. Test your knowledge and understanding by working through the online quiz in the Week 2 folder. Make sure you contribute to your weekly discussion. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04

Week 2: Making confident word choices In this tutorial, you'll complete some hands-on activities to introduce you to the English word classes. You'll apply some principles of word choice to consider accessibility, voice, and genre. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04
Week 3: READING WEEK Due to the Ekka Holiday, which falls on a Wednesday, this week is a reading week in the course.

Week 4: Determiners and nouns – the sentence subject To prepare for your classes this week, read The Writer's Diet — ‘Noun density’, watch the 'Zombie nouns' video in the Week 4 folder, and work through the other resources published there. BEFORE CLASS, WATCH THESE PRIMER VIDEOS What is the subject position in an English sentence? What kind of elements can sit in subject position? What is subject–verb agreement? What are determiners (articles, demonstratives, possessives, quantifiers)? What's a noun? FACE-TO-FACE LECTURE Sub-categories of nouns: nominalisations, common, proper, concrete, abstract, collective, and compound nouns Count vs non-count nouns and their patterns of use How noun choices can impact tone, precision, and clarity Test your knowledge and understanding by working through the online quiz in the Week 4 folder. Make sure you contribute to your weekly discussion. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04

Week 4: Using nouns effectively In this tutorial, you'll complete some hands-on activities to help you better understand sentence subjects in English and the structure of a noun phrase. You'll practise identifying nouns in context, describing the way an author might use them to achieve different effects, and some standard conventions to master as an editor. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04

Week 5: Pronouns and adjectives – the sentence object To prepare for classes this week, read The Writer's Diet — ‘Waste words’, as well as the other resources in the Week 5 folder. BEFORE CLASS, WATCH THESE PRIMER VIDEOS What's a sentence object in English? What's a sentence complement? What's a pronoun? What's an adjective? FACE-TO-FACE LECTURE Personal, possessive, reflexive, relative, and indefinite pronouns Pronoun reference, agreement, and case Attributive vs predicative adjectives Degrees of comparison and adjective ordering Creating precision using pronouns and adjectives Test your knowledge and understanding by working through the online quiz in the Week 5 folder. Make sure you contribute to your weekly discussion. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04

Week 5: Using pronouns and adjectives In this tutorial, you'll complete some hands-on activities to help you integrate pronouns and adjectives seamlessly into your writing. You'll practise identifying pronouns and adjectives in context, describing the way an author might use these parts of speech to add colour and precision to their writing, and some standard conventions to master as an editor. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04

Week 6: Verbs – the sentence 'pivot' To prepare for your classes, read The Writer's Diet — ‘Verbal verve’, as well as the other resources in the Week 6 folder. BEFORE CLASS, WATCH THESE PRIMER VIDEOS What is a finite verb? Why are finite verbs the 'heart' of a predicate – and an English sentence as a whole? How do finite verbs agree with a subject? What are transitive, intransitive, and linking verbs? What's an adverb? FACE-TO-FACE LECTURE The anatomy of English verb phrases Main vs auxiliary verbs Basics of verb tense and aspect Test your knowledge and understanding by working through the online quiz in the Week 6 folder. Make sure you contribute to your weekly discussion. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04

Week 6: Using verbs In this tutorial, you'll complete some hands-on activities to help you integrate strong, muscular verbs into your writing. You'll practise identifying finite and non-finite verbs in context, as well as understanding the structure of a verb phrase, describing the way an author might manipulate verb tense and aspect in their writing, and applying standard conventions as an editor. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04

Week 7: Verbs and verbals – continued To prepare for your classes, read The Writer's Diet — ‘Ad-dictions’, as well as the other resources in the Week 7 folder. BEFORE CLASS, WATCH THESE PRIMER VIDEOS How and when do we form active and passive voice in English? What are phrasal or multi-word verbs? FACE-TO-FACE LECTURE Non-finite verb forms and their surprising functions Adverb types and functions Adverb placement and its effect on clarity/meaning Using adverbs wisely 3 common modifier problems and how to avoid them Test your knowledge and understanding by working through the online quiz in the Week 7 folder. Make sure you contribute to your weekly discussion. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04

Week 7: Understanding voice and using non-finite verb forms In this tutorial, you'll consider the communicative options available to you when choosing between active and passive voice. You'll practise identifying non-finite verb forms in context and the ways they add extra action, dynamism, and dimension to our sentences. You'll also consider the ways authors use adverbs in their writing – and some additional conventions to be aware of as an editor, especially by avoiding misused modifiers. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04

Week 8: Connections and relationships – English function words To prepare for your classes, read The Writer's Diet — ‘Prepositional podge’, as well as the other resources in the Week 8 folder. BEFORE CLASS, WATCH THESE PRIMER VIDEOS What are prepositions, and how do they show connections between other words in a sentence? Which words belong to the conjunction class? FACE-TO-FACE LECTURE Function words and their effect on sentence structure and flow Common preposition problems Coordinating, subordinating, and correlative conjunctions Main vs subordinate clauses Polysyndeton and conjunctive adverbs Test your knowledge and understanding by working through the online quiz in the Week 8 folder. Make sure you contribute to your weekly discussion. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04

Week 8: Using function words In this tutorial, you'll practise expanding and combining clauses by using prepositional phrases and coordinating/subordinating conjunctions. You'll work on identifying different sentence types and consider how authors play with sentence structure to achieve a variety of semantic and aesthetic effects in their writing. You'll also practise editing writing at the sentence level to resolve common errors and weaknesses. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04
Week 9: NO LECTURE
Week 9: Tutorial problem set In this tutorial, you'll complete your in-class assessment activity: analysing, discussing, and responding to a passage of text. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04
IN-SEMESTER BREAK

Week 10: Clauses and sentences To prepare for your classes, read ThoughtCo ‘Sentence Definition and Examples in English Grammar’, as well as the other resources in the Week 10 folder. BEFORE CLASS, WATCH THESE PRIMER VIDEOS What is a sentence? (What's the difference between a clause and a sentence?) What structures can we choose from when writing an English sentence? What is grammatical mood? FACE-TO FACE LECTURE Independent vs dependent clauses (subordinate, relative, and content clauses) Simple, compound, complex, and compound-complex sentences Sentence weight and branching Restrictive vs non-restrictive clauses Creating sentence variety Test your knowledge and understanding by working through the online quiz in the Week 10 folder. Make sure you contribute to your weekly discussion. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04

Week 10: Making and refining sentences In this tutorial, you'll practise identifying various permutations of an English sentence and consider some of the ways authors might choose to manipulate elements such as sentence length, mood, and branching/weighting to communicate clearly, modulate pace, achieve variety, and create emphasis. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04

Week 11: Sentences in sequence To prepare for classes this week, start reading The Briefest Grammar and Punctuation Guide Ever! , as well as Steven Pinker's 'Coherence relations' passage and the other resources in the Week 11 folder. BEFORE CLASS, WATCH THESE PRIMER VIDEOS What can we distil from our learning so far as an editing checklist for strong, effective sentences? What are some common sentence-level errors we can weed out in carefully edited text? FACE-TO-FACE LECTURE Natural paragraph variation within and across text types Achieving clarity, coherence, and cohesion at the macro level Coherence relations Test your knowledge and understanding by working through the online quiz in the Week 11 folder. Make sure you contribute to your weekly discussion. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04

Week 11: Writing and editing at the paragraph level In this tutorial, you'll sharpen your writing and editing skills by considering coherence and cohesion when combining sentences. You'll also apply your knowledge of common sentence-level errors to refine passages of text for different audiences and purposes. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04

Week 12: Applying punctuation for accuracy and rhetorical effect To prepare for classes this week, finish reading The Briefest Grammar and Punctuation Guide Ever! , as well as the other resouces in the Week 12 folder. BEFORE CLASS, WATCH THESE PRIMER VIDEOS Where did punctuation come from, and why is it important? Are there right and wrong ways to punctuate? How do we apply a style guide to make decisions about punctuation? FACE-TO-FACE LECTURE Punctuation quandaries for professional writers and editors Accessibility conventions in contemporary edited English Principles of sound document design Test your knowledge and understanding by working through the online quiz in the Week 12 folder. Make sure you contribute to your weekly discussion. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04

Week 12: Copyediting to strengthen punctuation In this tutorial, you'll get some hands-on experience editing passages of text to make sure their punctuation is accurate, consistent, and elegant. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04

Week 13: Course reflection and advanced stylistic techniques BEFORE CLASS, WATCH THESE PRIMER VIDEOS How do LLMs and chatbots work? What implications does GenAI have for writers and editors? How can we use grammar for good? FACE-TO-FACE LECTURE Linguistic variety: how English grammars differ across Australia and the world Final takeaways: what explicit knowledge of English grammar can add to our writing and editing toolkits Test your knowledge and understanding by working through the online quiz in the Week 13 folder. Make sure you contribute to your final weekly discussion. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04

Week 13: Course reflection and editing workshop In this tutorial, you'll look back over your semester of learning and work through an editing task, to prepare you for your final assessment item in the course. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04
